Pi-score and p-value adjustment

Source: vignettes/scoring.Rmd
scoring.Rmd
library(enrichVolcano)

The problem with ranking by p-value alone

A p-value answers a single question: how surprising is this effect under the null. It says nothing about how big the effect is. In proteomics this matters because two proteins can carry the same p-value while telling different biological stories.

Consider two rows from a hypothetical limma output:

gene logFC P.Value -log10(P)
A 0.10 1e-6 6.0
B 2.50 1e-3 3.0

By raw p-value, A wins by three orders of magnitude. A 10% change in abundance, however, is rarely the headline story in a muscle biopsy. B has 5.6-fold higher absolute log fold change and a p-value that would still pass most cut-offs. Ranking by -log10(p) alone puts A on top; ranking by |logFC| alone puts B on top. Neither ranking is right on its own.

Xiao Y et al. (2014, Bioinformatics 30(6):801) proposed combining the two into a single ranking score. They called it pi-score and gave two equivalent forms. This package implements both.

Pi-score: two variants

Equation 2 (default)

πEq2=P|log⁡2FC| \pi_{\text{Eq2}} = P^{|\log_2 \text{FC}|}

Range: [0,1][0, 1]. Smaller pi means stronger evidence (p is small and logFC is large). The convention threshold is 0.05, mirroring the familiar p-value threshold.

This is the form used in the YvO, CvH, HRvLR, and Mito pipelines that ship as fixtures with this package. pi_score() defaults to it because the [0, 1] range plays well with downstream cut-offs that already expect a probability-like quantity.

example <- tibble::tibble(
  gene    = c("A", "B"),
  logFC   = c(0.10, 2.50),
  P.Value = c(1e-6, 1e-3)
)
pi_score(example, variant = "eq2")
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   gene  logFC  P.Value       pi_eq2
#>   <chr> <dbl>    <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 A       0.1 0.000001 0.251       
#> 2 B       2.5 0.001    0.0000000316

By Eq.2, B has the smaller pi (better) even though its raw p is larger. The exponentiation by |logFC| shrinks A’s tiny p when the effect is small.

Equation 1 (alternative)

πEq1=|log⁡2FC|×−log⁡10P \pi_{\text{Eq1}} = |\log_2 \text{FC}| \times -\log_{10} P

Range: [0,∞)[0, \infty). Larger pi means stronger evidence. Same paper, same authors, just the other equation in the original text.

pi_score(example, variant = "eq1")
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   gene  logFC  P.Value pi_eq1
#>   <chr> <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 A       0.1 0.000001    0.6
#> 2 B       2.5 0.001       7.5

Eq.1 gives 0.10 * 6 = 0.6 for A and 2.50 * 3 = 7.5 for B. B again beats A, by a wider margin than Eq.2 gives.

Worked numerical example

Drop the formula into a calculator with logFC = 2 and P = 0.01:

  • Eq.2: 0.01|2|=0.00010.01^{|2|} = 0.0001
  • Eq.1: |2|×−log⁡10(0.01)=2×2=4|2| \times -\log_{10}(0.01) = 2 \times 2 = 4

Now nudge the effect down to logFC = 0.5 with the same p:

  • Eq.2: 0.01|0.5|=0.10.01^{|0.5|} = 0.1
  • Eq.1: |0.5|×−log⁡10(0.01)=0.5×2=1|0.5| \times -\log_{10}(0.01) = 0.5 \times 2 = 1

Cutting the effect in half multiplies Eq.2 by 1000 and divides Eq.1 by 4. Both penalise small effects, but Eq.2 is more aggressive.

Choosing a variant

Use Eq.2 when downstream code expects a [0, 1] scale (significance flags, FDR-like cut-offs, sortable as a p-value). Use Eq.1 when you need to compare against a paper that reports unbounded pi values. For fgsea ranking, the two variants rank-order genes the same way as long as every raw p is below 1 (which is always true in practice). For ORA, only the [0, 1] form has a natural significance threshold.

Both ignore the sign of logFC, so they collapse up- and down-regulation onto the same axis. If you need direction-aware ranking (the standard input to fgsea), pass rank_by = "logFC" to ev_enrich(). The pi-score is for filtering and labelling, not for GSEA pre-ranking.

Multiple-testing correction overview

adjust_p() accepts four methods. They differ in what they control and how much power you keep.

Benjamini-Hochberg (default)

BH controls the false discovery rate: the expected proportion of false positives among rejected hypotheses. It is the proteomics field default because it gives more power than Bonferroni at a biologically defensible error rate. stats::p.adjust(p, "BH") is the implementation.

Bonferroni

Bonferroni controls the family-wise error rate: the probability of any false positive. Multiplies each p by the number of tests. With 3000 proteins this is severe; a raw p of 1e-5 ends up at 0.03. Use this when you need to confirm a small set of pre-selected biomarkers, not for screening.

Storey q-value

The q-value method (Storey 2003, JRSS-B 64:479) estimates the proportion of true null hypotheses (π0\pi_0) and weights BH by it. When most proteins are truly null, π̂0\hat\pi_0 is close to 1 and the result matches BH. When many proteins really do change (a strong treatment), π̂0\hat\pi_0 is below 1 and the q-value beats BH on power. Requires the qvalue package from Bioconductor.

IHW

Independent Hypothesis Weighting (Ignatiadis et al. 2016, Nature Methods 13:577) is BH with informative weights. You supply a covariate that is independent of the p-value under the null but correlated with power under the alternative. In proteomics, peptide count per protein is a good covariate: more peptides means a more precise estimate, so a small p with high peptide count is more trustworthy than a small p with one peptide. adjust_p() accepts covariate = "peptides" (or any numeric column) and calls IHW::ihw().

Choosing in practice

Most proteomics papers report BH. q-value is a free-lunch upgrade when you have a treatment with global effects. IHW is the best choice when you have a per-protein covariate that predicts power; otherwise it reduces to BH.

Worked example with the YvO subsample 

fixture <- system.file(
  "extdata", "examples", "yvo_tidy.rds",
  package = "enrichVolcano"
)
if (!nzchar(fixture)) {
  fixture <- "../tests/testthat/fixtures/yvo_tidy.rds"
}
yvo <- readRDS(fixture)
yvo <- yvo[!is.na(yvo$gene) & !is.na(yvo$contrast), ]
nrow(yvo)
#> [1] 400

Compute pi-scores both ways and look at the rank correlation within the Aging contrast:

yvo <- pi_score(yvo, variant = "eq2")
yvo <- pi_score(yvo, variant = "eq1")
aging <- yvo[yvo$contrast == "Aging", ]
cor(rank(aging$pi_eq2), rank(-aging$pi_eq1))
#> [1] 1

The correlation is essentially 1: -pi_eq1 and pi_eq2 rank rows identically. The two are interchangeable for ordering; they differ only in scale.

Now compare BH and Bonferroni at α=0.05\alpha = 0.05:

yvo_bh   <- adjust_p(yvo, method = "BH")
yvo_bonf <- adjust_p(yvo, method = "bonferroni")
sig_bh   <- sum(yvo_bh$adj.P.Val   < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
sig_bonf <- sum(yvo_bonf$adj.P.Val < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
c(BH = sig_bh, Bonferroni = sig_bonf)
#>         BH Bonferroni 
#>        219         73

BH calls roughly an order of magnitude more proteins significant than Bonferroni, at the cost of allowing a few false positives among the rejected nulls. For a screening workflow that feeds into pathway enrichment, that trade-off is the right one.

adjust_p() adjusts within each contrast by default (by_contrast = TRUE). This matches the proteoDA convention: a training response and an aging effect are independent families and should not share an error budget.

References

Xiao Y, Hsiao TH, Suresh U, Chen HIH, Wu X, Wolf SE, Chen Y. A novel significance score for gene identification from RNA-seq data. Bioinformatics 30(6):801-807 (2014).

Benjamini Y, Hochberg Y. Controlling the false discovery rate: a practical and powerful approach to multiple testing. JRSS-B 57(1):289-300 (1995).

Storey JD. The positive false discovery rate: a Bayesian interpretation and the q-value. Annals of Statistics 31(6):2013-2035 (2003).

Ignatiadis N, Klaus B, Zaugg JB, Huber W. Data-driven hypothesis weighting increases detection power in genome-scale multiple testing. Nature Methods 13(7):577-580 (2016).
